attempts.raw_response: He quickly distinguished himself as a prodigious talent, winning numerous competitions throughout his teenage years. At seventeen, he made his debut with the New York Philharmonic, performing the Paganini Concerto No. 1 under the baton of Leonard Bernstein. Critics praised his technical brilliance and emotionally rich tone. He went on to win the prestigious Naumburg Award in 1965, which launched his international career. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, he performed as a soloist with major orchestras worldwide, including the Boston Symphony, the Chicago Symphony, and the Philadelphia Orchestra. His recordings earned multiple Grammy Awards. He became known for his interpretations of the Romantic concerto repertoire, particularly the works of Brahms, Tchaikovsky, and Mendelssohn. Teaching also became important to him later in his career, and he joined the faculty at Juilliard, following in the footsteps of his legendary teachers.

pair.human_continuation:
His Carnegie Hall debut took place in January 1950, at the age of 13, as soloist with the National Orchestral Association, playing Vieuxtemps' Concerto No. 5 under the direction of Léon Barzin. Subsequently, he appeared with a number of American orchestras before his Carnegie Hall debut on 29 November 1951, at the age of 15, in the Paganini D major Concerto, with Dimitri Mitropoulos conducting the New York Philharmonic. His 1958 recording of this concerto is considered by many to be the most impressive recording of this work, and the recording itself is notable for the fullness of tone.

His first London appearance took place on 13 December 1954, at age 18, playing the Tchaikovsky Concerto in D at the Royal Albert Hall with the BBC Symphony Orchestra.
pair.prefix: His mother Jeanne was a Juilliard-trained pianist, and his father George was a violinist in the New York Philharmonic. He began to study the violin at the age of seven. His parents encouraged his musical development. After a lesson with Jascha Heifetz, the master advised him to study with Ivan Galamian, who said he had "no weaknesses, never." He began studies with Galamian in New York and at the Meadowmount School of Music and the Juilliard School.
